rationale: Explanation written by Claude. Method 1 — solve for c, then evaluate. Substitute x = 2 into the definition: g(2) = 5(2) + c(2 + 4) = 10 + 6c Set that equal to the given value: 10 + 6c = 46 → 6c = 36 → c = 6 Now evaluate at x = 5: g(5) = 5(5) + 6(5 + 4) = 25 + 6(9) = 25 + 54 = 79 Method 2 — direct difference (faster, no need to isolate c). Expand once: g(x) = 5x + cx + 4c = (5 + c)x + 4c. This is linear in x with slope (5 + c), so g(5) − g(2) = (5 + c)(5 − 2) = 3(5 + c) You still need c, but note the slope shortcut is only a win once c is known — from 10 + 6c = 46, c = 6, so slope = 11 and g(5) = 46 + 3(11) = 46 + 33 = 79 . Where this goes wrong on test day. The two common errors are (1) distributing c only onto x and forgetting the +4c term, and (2) solving for c correctly but then plugging x = 5 back into the original g(2) equation instead of re-evaluating. Both use "expanses'" — a plural possessive — after the singular "this swampy." Wrong number, so both are out regardless of what happens to "road." Step 3: Decide whether "road" is possessive. "Road" is the last noun in the phrase; nothing follows that it could own. A possessive must be followed by the thing possessed. "This swampy expanse's road's" leaves "road's" owning nothing — a fragment of a phrase. Step 4: Eliminate A. A has the correct singular possessive "expanse's" but adds a stray apostrophe to "road's," creating exactly that ownerless possessive. Step 5: Confirm D. "This swampy expanse's roads" reads correctly: singular possessive "expanse's" (the roads belonging to the one swampy expanse, i.e. the Darien Gap) followed by the simple plural "roads." The later pronoun "it" — "ferry around it " — also confirms the singular expanse as the referent. Reading & Writing · Medium · Standard English Conventions · Form, Structure, and Sense
